extracted.intended_audience: students and general readers of American government / political science
extracted.subtask_description: Analytic summary of institutional norms and practical causes shaping the U.S. Congress (residency expectations, salaries, tenure, committee work, leadership, attendance, size). Intended as explanatory material on why Congress functions as it does.

rubrics_metrics.name: Residency expectation for representatives
rubrics_metrics.description: Constituencies expect their chosen representatives to reside within their district or locality; local feeling deems no man fit to represent who has not by residence become soaked with local sentiment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explained as stemming from historically separate States and strong local government habits; local sympathy and analogy foster the view that an outsider cannot properly represent local interests. Examples/notes: Americans view this as natural, whereas English practice often allows non-resident representation; anecdotes (candidate laughed at for not living in district) illustrate strength of the norm.

rubrics_metrics.name: State-based representation for senators
rubrics_metrics.description: A senator is effectively an ambassador of his State and is expected to be a resident of that State; chosen by the legislature or collective authority of the State.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: divided allegiance would be problematic if senator resided in another State. Compared with other countries where members sometimes sit for places where they do not reside (England, France, Germany, Canada), though residence gives some advantage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Local comprehension as qualification for advocacy
rubrics_metrics.description: It is thought that only an inhabitant can duly comprehend the needs of a locality or zealously advocate its demands (e.g., regarding tariffs, appropriations, harbour works, river navigation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is offered as a cause of preference for local representatives: local issues (economic and infrastructural) are believed to require local knowledge and zeal. This belief supports electoral preference for residents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rewarding local political work with seats
rubrics_metrics.description: Because the congressional post is paid and local political work (organizing, canvassing, haranguing) keeps parties going, constituencies feel a good position ought to be kept for one of themselves rather than given to a stranger.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains cultural/political expectation that local activists should be rewarded; contributes to preference for local candidates even when higher statesmanship might be desirable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate numerical size of representation
rubrics_metrics.description: There is debate over the number of representatives (e.g., one per 30,000 historically) balancing the need for every small district to be heard against the confusion and infirmities of very numerous assemblies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Federalist argument quoted: enough members needed for free consultation and local information, but numbers must be limited to avoid confusion, passion, and domination by the few. Practical American worries: House may already be too large and risk disorganization if growth continues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permitting representation across different parts of a State
rubrics_metrics.description: Questioning the reason for preventing a resident of one part of a State from representing another part (e.g., a New Yorker representing Pittsburg): in Europe non-resident representation is common and can be successful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argument: non-resident representatives can be more persuasive or personally influential; in conflicts of interest they feel obligations first to constituents rather than to place of residence. The American habit against this is stronger and rooted in local government traditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Payment/remuneration of members
rubrics_metrics.description: Members receive a salary (and allowances) justified as compensation for lost livelihood and travel expenses; payment is necessary to enable attendance and continuous service at Washington.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effects discussed: payment helps sustain attendance but may foster a class of professional politicians; it was not primarily introduced to enable working men to serve; European conditions differ, so American experience isn't directly transferable. Cynical view noted ('they would steal worse if they didn't get it').

rubrics_metrics.name: Tenure length and its trade-offs (two-year House terms)
rubrics_metrics.description: Short tenure (House: two years) produces frequent turnover and inexperienced members, while intended as a democratic check and to keep popular interest; it also limits members' ability to master laws and study problems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical context: many State constitutions had one-year terms; Federalists argued two years were needed for mastery. Present effect: frequent elections mean many new members, reducing continuity and efficiency; countervailing argument: frequent elections check the President and keep members responsive to constituents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Re-election pressures and constituency 'nursing'
rubrics_metrics.description: Members face continuous pressure to secure re-nomination and re-election by procuring federal grants, posts for friends/relatives, and by 'nursing' the constituency during vacations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Result: discourages high statesmanship and the cultivation of expertise; encourages attention to local/personal interests (places, patronage) rather than broader public policy; career interruptions occur when ambitious politicians cannot find seats elsewhere.

rubrics_metrics.name: Committee-centrality of substantive legislative work
rubrics_metrics.description: Most serious legislative work is done in committees rather than in full dress debates; committee work is often unknown to the public and many committee-considered bills never reach a House vote.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implications: opportunities for public distinction are limited; committee positions are obtained by favour; ability, tact, and industry pay off only in the long run, but many members never have a long run due to turnover.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attendance and quorum requirements encourage presence
rubrics_metrics.description: A high constitutional quorum requirement (one-half) and long travel distances to Washington contribute to comparatively assiduous attendance by American congressmen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contrasts with British Houses with lower quorums and poorer attendance. Other causes: members do not usually carry on regular business during sessions; the sergeant-at-arms may even fetch members when needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lack of centralized party leadership and the role of whips
rubrics_metrics.description: Traditionally there were no recognized leaders or regularly working agencies for managing party votes; the whip (when present) performs vital tasks: informing members of divisions, directing votes, obtaining pairs, counting members, and keeping the leader informed of party opinion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Full list of whip duties provided: (1) inform members when divisions expected and keep them present; (2) direct party voting; (3) obtain pairs for absentees; (4) 'tell' (count) members in divisions; (5) keep touch of opinion within the party and report to the leader. Failure to respond to the whip's summons is a serious breach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limited opportunities for public distinction in Congress
rubrics_metrics.description: Congress offers few opportunities for members to gain public distinction; full debates are rare, newspaper reports of speeches are curt, and the institution is not a major social or cultural focus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consequences: fewer ambitious men seek Congressional careers compared with law, education, commerce, or finance; the Senate and Federal judges overshadow representatives in status; members' social standing is modest, especially in the North.
